clue.text: Where a member uses one, of course

definitions.text: Where a member uses one, of course

blocks.note: surface reading: the place a person who has joined something goes
setter's reading: the same two words name both a members' club for the sport and the stick each player swings on the course

explanation.surface: A puzzle about where a member of some society goes and what they use there.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer means both the clubhouse a member belongs to and the iron or wood they swing on the course.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf club is at once a sporting association with members and the implement swung during play on a course.

clue.text: Visible in fog, as little Fanny was

definitions.note: a clause describing how Fanny was seen, standing for the adjective

indicators.note: something visible in the next words can be seen sitting among their letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of fog, the whole of as and the start of little

explanation.surface: A little girl called Fanny glimpsed through a foggy Victorian street.
explanation.walkthrough: Fanny by Gaslight is a 1940s British film and novel set in Victorian London, where streets were lit by gas lamps.
explanation.definitionFit: The title Fanny by Gaslight says the heroine was seen by the glow of coal-gas street lamps.

clue.text: Cricket ground joints for those hearing appeals

definitions.note: a form of address for judges, standing for the judges themselves

blocks.note: Lord's is the famous London cricket ground
hips are joints of the body

explanation.surface: Bones and venues for cricketers, with cricket appeals to the umpire suggested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appeals' suggests a bowler shouting at an umpire, but these appeals are legal ones heard in the House of Lords.
explanation.definitionFit: Judges and Law Lords are addressed as 'my lord', so their lordships are the people who hear legal appeals.

clue.text: Jungle fighter, note, bides in middle of hedge

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter, so only that one is kept
the note abides round the following letters, holding them as it stays in place

blocks.note: a chit is a short written note
taken as written
the central letter of hedge

explanation.surface: A soldier in the jungle writes a note while waiting inside a hedge.
explanation.walkthrough: The Chindits were British special forces who fought behind Japanese lines in the Burmese jungle in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Chindits were long-range infantry raiders operating in the Burmese jungle, so one of them is a jungle fighter.

clue.text: Assistant giving lessons in pronouns

blocks.note: two pronouns, the first person plural object and the third person feminine object, side by side

explanation.surface: A teaching assistant giving lessons on grammar, specifically pronouns.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is US + HER. An usher was an old word for a school's assistant master.
explanation.definitionFit: In older British schools an under-master who helped the headmaster teach pupils was called by this title.

clue.text: Striker said in this game . . .

indicators.note: said tells us to go by how the word for a striker is spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: one who socks, or hits, someone is a striker

explanation.surface: A striker, the attacking footballer, speaking during a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striker' looks like the football position but means a person who socks or punches. The dots run on into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Association football, the sport with strikers, is commonly called by this name, especially in America.

clue.text: Ran into Emperor in Italian castle

indicators.note: going into something puts these letters inside the next word

blocks.note: taken as written
Otto was the name of several Holy Roman Emperors

explanation.surface: Someone collided with an emperor inside a castle in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Castle of Otranto is Horace Walpole's 1764 novel, the first Gothic novel, named after a real castle in Apulia.
explanation.definitionFit: Otranto is a town in southern Italy whose castle gave its name to Walpole's famous Gothic novel.

clue.text: National obstacle to preside over

blocks.note: first meaning: the tallest fence on the Grand National course at Aintree
second meaning: to run a meeting

explanation.surface: Something blocking the nation from presiding over its affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grand National is Britain's most famous steeplechase horse race, and one of its jumps is named The Chair.
explanation.definitionFit: The fence called The Chair is a hurdle in the National, and to take the chair is to lead a meeting.

clue.text: Enigmatic way of shooting full of holes

definitions.text: way of shooting full of holes
definitions.note: a verb form naming the act

blocks.note: first meaning: speaking in puzzles

blocks.clueFragment: way of shooting full of holes
blocks.note: second meaning: perforating with bullets, like a sieve

explanation.surface: A mysterious gunman with an odd method of peppering a target.
explanation.walkthrough: A riddle is both a puzzle and a coarse sieve, so the verb covers speaking puzzlingly and perforating.
explanation.definitionFit: Speech full of puzzles is cryptic and mysterious, and a target peppered with bullets has been pierced through like a sieve.

clue.text: Not prepared to say how Alice met her fiance

definitions.note: the second reading is a phrase describing circumstances

blocks.note: first meaning: caught unready
second meaning: in A. A. Milne's poem, Alice is marrying one of the soldiers at Buckingham Palace, so she met him when he was not on duty

explanation.surface: Someone caught unready to explain how Alice met her husband-to-be.
explanation.walkthrough: A. A. Milne's poem 'Buckingham Palace' has the line 'Alice is marrying one of the guard'; she would have met him while he was off duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Caught unprepared is the idiom, and a guardsman free from sentry duty is literally away from his post.

clue.text: ... to be an honest player without complications

blocks.note: a straight dealer is an honest one
a forward is an attacking player in football, continuing the game of the previous clue

explanation.surface: Continuing the football theme: it pays to be an honest player in the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Something simple and uncomplicated is plain and direct to deal with, the idiomatic sense of the phrase.

clue.text: One who's joined group in drink, say

indicators.note: say asks for a word that sounds right when spoken rather than spelt right

blocks.note: taken as written
cider is an apple drink

explanation.surface: A new member of a group celebrates by having a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A person admitted to a circle or organisation is on the inside of it, a member with privileged knowledge.

clue.text: Female played terrible role in king's end

definitions.note: names the character as a role that is performed

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that is kept
something terrible is in a dreadful state, so the following letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the final letter of king
taken as written, to be mixed

explanation.surface: An actress gave a terrible performance at the end of a play about a king.
explanation.walkthrough: Goneril is one of King Lear's two wicked daughters, and 'king's end' hints at Lear's tragic end too.
explanation.definitionFit: Goneril is a woman's role in Shakespeare's King Lear, a part taken by an actress on stage.

clue.text: Falls down under part of carriage

blocks.note: first meaning: the great waterfall on the Zambezi
second meaning: a state of Australia, the land 'down under'
third meaning: a light four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage

explanation.surface: Something tumbles down beneath part of a carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings: the Falls in Africa, the Australian state, and a horse-drawn carriage named after the queen.
explanation.definitionFit: The Zambezi waterfall, the southeastern Australian state and a low open horse carriage all share the queen's name.

clue.text: Those who take corners in this game?

blocks.note: first meaning: people who go round bends
second meaning: a bat-and-ball game where players run round bases

explanation.surface: Players taking corner kicks in a football game.
explanation.walkthrough: Corners suggest football; rounders is a British bat-and-ball game like baseball, in which runners do go round corners.
explanation.definitionFit: People who round corners are rounders, and rounders is a schoolyard bat-and-ball game resembling baseball.

clue.text: Artist or writer

blocks.note: taken as written
a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone is a painter or an author.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir William Orpen was an Irish portrait painter and official war artist in the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: William Orpen was a celebrated Irish portrait painter, so his surname names a particular artist.

clue.text: Closest companion supports no amateur team

indicators.note: in a down clue what supports sits underneath, so the companion goes at the bottom

blocks.note: someone who is not an amateur is a professional
a football or cricket team has eleven players, written XI
a mate is a companion

explanation.surface: A best friend backs a team that is not amateur.
explanation.definitionFit: Proximate means nearest or immediately next, as in a proximate cause, so it fits closest.

clue.text: Last part of church conceded as sanctified

indicators.note: the last part of a word is its final letter, which alone is taken

blocks.note: the final letter of church
to concede a point is to allow it

explanation.surface: The end of a church service grudgingly recognised as holy.
explanation.definitionFit: Hallowed ground is made holy by consecration, the same sense as sanctified.

clue.text: Change for Romans to be such fools

blocks.note: first meaning: the as was a Roman copper coin, so several are Roman loose change
second meaning: stupid people, as donkeys are proverbially

explanation.surface: Romans being told that changing their ways would make them fools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' suggests altering something; here it means coins, and the as was a small Roman bronze coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Stupid people are called donkeys, the plural being the same word as the coins.

clue.text: Person who breaks dish

blocks.note: first meaning: one who shatters things
second meaning: an attractive person, informally

explanation.surface: Someone in the kitchen who breaks a plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish' looks like crockery being broken but is slang for a good-looking person; a smasher is British slang for the same.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a very attractive or excellent person is a smasher, just as a good-looking one is a dish.

clue.text: Make rare good opening as the likely loser

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: to cook meat lightly, leaving it rare, is to underdo it
the first letter of good

explanation.surface: Advice that a rare good opening move suits the competitor tipped to lose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rare' suggests unusual, but here it is the steak sense.
explanation.definitionFit: In a contest the competitor expected to be beaten is called the underdog by tipsters and fans.

clue.text: Philosopher said to take stock

indicators.note: said means the word is to be heard spoken, not seen spelt

blocks.note: to rustle is to steal livestock

explanation.surface: A thinker reportedly paused to take stock of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take stock' suggests reflecting; here stock means cattle, and taking them is rustling.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertrand Russell was a leading twentieth-century British logician and philosopher.

clue.text: Left as resort's in holiday mood

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase for the adjective

indicators.note: read as re-sort, meaning sort the letters again into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be mixed

explanation.surface: Someone departed feeling cheerful, as a seaside resort is in the holiday season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' suggests a holiday town, which fits the surface, but it is re-sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Festal means relating to a feast or festival, hence festive and in a holiday spirit.

clue.text: He gets behind to pull girl back

indicators.note: back tells us to read the combined letters in the other direction

blocks.note: to drag is to pull
gal is an informal word for a girl

explanation.surface: A man trailing behind a girl, trying to pull her back.
explanation.definitionFit: A slowcoach who falls behind the rest is a straggler, a dawdler who lags.

clue.text: Minimum quantity of dye

blocks.note: first meaning: the smallest unit of weight, or a tiny amount
second meaning: an old name for the red cochineal or kermes dye

explanation.surface: Just a tiny amount of dye is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: Kermes insects looked like seeds, so the red dye made from them was called by the seed's name; 'dyed in the grain' meant colourfast.
explanation.definitionFit: The smallest unit in the troy and avoirdupois weight systems shares a name with an old crimson insect dye.

clue.text: Recreation period of older generation

blocks.note: first meaning: a hobby
second meaning, read punningly as two words: a bygone time

explanation.surface: The leisure activity favoured by older people.
explanation.walkthrough: Split apart, the answer reads as 'past time', the era of an older generation.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobby enjoyed in spare hours is a recreation, which makes the time pass pleasantly.

clue.text: Disposed of 15's composition

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so the letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: the answer to clue 15, the painter

explanation.surface: Something disposed of by an earlier clue's composition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disposed of' looks like a phrase for getting rid of something; 'of' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Being prone to something means being inclined or liable to it, just as disposed to does.

clue.text: A shower etc after this, perhaps

definitions.text: A shower etc after this, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps admits the letters could take another form, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: every letter of these words, to be mixed

explanation.surface: A rain shower, among other things, arriving after a bulletin predicting it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the fodder: a shower and so on may follow the broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: A forecast predicts rain and sunshine, so showers may well come after it as promised.

clue.text: Is rand convertible into these?

definitions.note: a pronoun standing for the plural currency units

indicators.note: something convertible can be changed into another form, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, to be mixed

explanation.surface: Asking whether South African money can be exchanged for another currency.
explanation.walkthrough: The rand is South Africa's currency, and the answer is the currency of Middle Eastern and Balkan states.
explanation.definitionFit: Dinars are currency units of countries such as Jordan and Kuwait, the money one might change rand into.

clue.text: PM separately introducing same measure in confusion

indicators.note: separately means the two letters are split apart, each taking its own insert
introducing puts something in after each of the split letters

blocks.note: taken as written
an ell is an old measure of length for cloth
the same measure again

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister introducing the same measures in a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: PM looks like Prime Minister, but it is just two letters each followed by an ell.
explanation.definitionFit: Pell-mell means in a disorderly rush, headlong and jumbled together.
